title: In situ Electron Microscopy at Liquid Helium Temperatures
content: Quantum materials hold great promises for unconventional information science, such as quantum and neuromorphic computing, due to their emergent properties and collective behaviors that are not observed in noninteracting single-particle systems. Charge, spin, lattice, and orbital degrees of freedom and their interplay are at the heart of these quantum phenomena, leading to unique states of matter, including superconductivity, topological insulators, and quantum spin liquids, which can be harnessed for advanced technological applications beyond semiconductor-based microelectronics [1]. While average behaviors of these ingredients are being extensively studied in the momentum space, especially by x-ray scattering, local measurements and observations down to atomic scale are extremely limited. In this respect, in situ cryogenic transmission electron microscopy (cryo-TEM) holds great potential for quantum materials under external electric and magnetic fields at cryogenic temperatures, tailored for establishing structure-property relationships. This technique allows for the direct observation of local charge, spin, and lattice behaviors across structural phase transitions and their responses to external fields in the presence of inhomogeneities.
